name: Grace Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or political groups. This is confidential. Tell me about an ordinary day on your building site.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the carpentry end of a general building crew, mostly repairs and room conversions where no two walls quite match. I have a vocational trade certificate and know how to set out a stair, though I also use AI every day to tidy measurements into material lists. I'm fifty-eight; my partner and I have grown children, a few months of expenses saved and retirement on the calendar if the figures work. The pay is ordinary for the trade, and there are some other builders nearby, but I like this crew because they let me try a tool after I have checked it on a real job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI Plateau is a quieter version of the digital work we already do. A list can be faster, but someone still has to find the stud behind a finished wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I would welcome another steady year of carpentry pay. Our reserve covers a few months, not a long break, and I still need the wages for our hoped-for retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep leading repair and conversion work and check my AI material lists against a tape and the drawing. In the first year after the mild change, I'd add a small set amount from each full pay packet to our retirement savings if household bills allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened. The site looks steady, but only a few months of cash between us and a stopped wage is always in my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check your daily AI list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure the opening twice and compare it with the list before anyone orders the door. A neat AI list can still be wrong by a finger's width.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you make the extra deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would check the savings deposit against that month's bills. If a full pay packet leaves room, the extra deposit goes in; otherwise we keep the current balance.

say: **AI Plateau** would leave repair carpentry mostly familiar while digital material lists save a little time.
I would still put a **tape measure** against the actual opening before an order goes out.
think: I need **ordinary site pay** to keep our hoped-for retirement date within reach.
A **few months saved** helps, but would not carry us through a long wage gap.
do: **Keep** leading repairs and checking AI material lists against tape measurements.
**Add** a set amount to retirement savings from full pay packets only after bills are covered.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because our work looks steady but our cash reserve has limits.
S0.quote: A neat AI list can still be wrong by a finger's width.
fieldNote: She uses **AI daily** but treats site measurements as the final check.
Her moderate **cash reserve** and typical pay leave a real retirement timing concern even in a mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep leading repair carpentry and checking AI lists against site measurements
Add from full pay packets to retirement savings only after bills are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Steady Disruption will reach estimates, orders and bookings before it reaches the chisel in my hand. We should trial any new ordering tool on a small room before the whole crew has to live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can pick up a new screen, but a faster office might send fewer paid days to the site if jobs are priced too tightly. Retirement is close enough that losing one day a week would show in our figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the site manager for a paid one-room trial of the approved AI ordering tool, and join the builder's trade association discussion about checking time. If a paid trial is offered, I'd learn the tool on actual orders in the first year, compare deliveries with measured openings and keep my carpentry shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possible hours, though I have some control. I would rather test the system than complain about a screen I have never used on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the one-room trial measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count wrong door sizes and missing hinges on the first three deliveries. If the trial is not paid, I will not use my evenings to fix a builder's ordering system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you spot a cut in paid hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the next month's rota and compare paid days with the old one. A shorter week would send me to the household ledger before I agreed to any new title.

say: **Steady Disruption** would change estimates and orders before hands-on carpentry.
I would ask for a **paid small trial** before an AI ordering tool sets work for the whole crew.
think: A tighter **site rota** could trim my pay even if carpenters remain necessary.
I can learn software, but **retirement figures** depend on actual paid days.
do: **Request** a paid one-room trial of the approved AI ordering tool.
**Join** the trade association discussion on paid checking time.
**Learn** the tool on real orders only if a paid trial place is offered.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost days, with enough skill to test a new tool.
S1.quote: If the trial is not paid, I will not use my evenings to fix a builder's ordering system.
fieldNote: Her **trial request** is not an executed trial; use depends on an offered paid place.
She links a possible **shorter rota** directly to ordinary wages and her retirement figures.

steps.text: Join trade association discussion on paid checking time
Learn new AI ordering tool only if offered a paid trial place
Keep carpentry shifts and compare new rota with previous paid days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2028 could make plans and orders in two years, while capable hands-on building robots come around 2031. We need a safe site test before anyone cuts carpentry hours on a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty in 2028 I could still have several years of paid work ahead, and capable robots three years later might take some of it. A few months of savings is not a pension. I would consider site quality work, but only if the training and wage are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd request a paid supervised robot trial through the builder, and enrol in a recognised site-quality course only if the employer funds it with paid release and a place is offered. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep carpentry shifts, check AI plans against built walls and apply for posted local quality-inspector jobs after training only if their wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the dates put our planned savings years at risk. I can look for openings with the other local builders, but no advert is a wage packet yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe robot trial require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trial would need an operator stop control, marked exclusion space and a real uneven floor. If no paid supervised place is offered, my request stays a request.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test an inspector offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the posted inspector wage beside our housing and food costs, then ask about the actual start date. I will not count a quality job in our retirement plan until an offer has pay and hours in writing.

say: **AGI by 2028** would change site plans first, with capable hands-on robots around 2031.
I would seek **paid supervised trials** before the builder removes carpentry hours.
think: My final **earning years** could be cut by robot building while our reserve covers only months.
A **quality-inspector move** requires funded paid training and a real local offer at bill-covering wages.
do: **Request** a paid supervised robot trial with stop control, exclusion space and a real uneven floor.
**Enrol** in recognised site-quality training only with funded fees, paid release and an offered place.
**Apply** after training for posted local inspector jobs only at bill-covering wages.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing planned earnings, though I can still seek local work.
S2.quote: A few months of savings is not a pension.
fieldNote: She separates immediate **2028 planning** from the direct hands-on robot threat around 2031.
Her **trial, course and job** all require concrete offers, paid time, safety controls or bill-covering wages.

steps.text: Enrol in funded site-quality course only with paid release and offered place
Apply after training for posted local inspector job only at bill-covering wages
Keep carpentry shifts and check AI plans against built walls
Request paid supervised robot trial with stop control exclusion space and uneven floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2031 gives five years for thinking work and until around 2034 for capable building robots. That is time to prove where a quality inspector is needed, rather than invent a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three in 2031 I might be nearer retirement, but our few months of cash will not fund a sudden stop. A paid quality job could bridge the gap if it exists locally; if it does not, I need the carpentry shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask our builder for a funded recognised site-quality course and enrol only with an offered place and paid release. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep checking plans on the site and apply for a posted local inspector role only after completing training and confirming the pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later robot date, but five years give me time to check a real route. I can compare our retirement numbers with a posted wage instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the quality course useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether inspection includes authority to stop unsafe work and whether the course is recognised by nearby builders. A certificate with no local posting would sit unused in my drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How fixed is your retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would compare the budget at sixty-three with a later leaving date. We have a target, not a guaranteed pension date, and a missing wage could move it.

say: **AGI by 2031** gives five years before thinking AI and until around 2034 before capable building robots.
I would check a **real quality route** before leaving the carpentry rota.
think: Our **retirement date** is a target, not a guaranteed income once site pay stops.
A **local quality job** would help only after recognised funded training and an adequate written wage.
do: **Enrol** in recognised site-quality course only with employer funding, paid release and an offered place.
**Keep** checking plans against site work after 2031 while carpentry shifts continue.
**Apply** after training to posted local inspector work only if wages cover household bills.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later robots, with time to check a paid route.
S3.quote: A certificate with no local posting would sit unused in my drawer.
fieldNote: The **2034 robot date** gives her time, but not enough cash to abandon paid shifts.
She makes a **job application** separate from course completion, conditional on a posted local role and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Enrol in funded recognised site-quality course only with paid release and offered place
Keep carpentry shifts and check 2031 AI plans against site work
Apply after training for posted local inspector role only at bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 leaves ten years before thinking AI and until around 2039 before capable building robots. A decade is enough to keep records and train people, if builders actually pay for it. I would ask our builder for paid time to show apprentices the repair notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight in 2036, I hope to have left full-time site work, but that depends on ten years of wages and the savings plan holding. If our budget still needs income then, I may seek a part-time site-checking role instead of assuming retirement happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep leading repair jobs and add from full pay packets to our savings after bills, while recording the awkward measurements apprentices ask about. In the first year after 2036, if our retirement budget still needs a wage, I'd apply for a posted local part-time site-checking role only with safe duties and pay that fills the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because the long date gives us choices but no guaranteed income. I do like having time to leave useful measurements behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repair would go into your notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record the warped door frame, the measured opening and the adjustment we made. A carpentry apprentice can learn more from one corrected drawing than from a perfect sample.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you still need income after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would recalculate the gap after looking at our actual savings and any retirement payments then available. If the gap is zero, I would leave the paid rota rather than invent a part-time job.

say: **AGI by 2036** allows a decade before thinking AI changes plans and longer before capable building robots.
I would ask builders to fund **paid teaching time** for practical site knowledge.
think: Retirement by **2036** is possible only if current wages and savings meet our budget.
A **part-time site role** would be a fallback if paid work is still needed.
do: **Keep** leading repair jobs and recording awkward site measurements for apprentices.
**Add** from full pay packets to savings only after bills are covered.
**Apply** after 2036 for posted local part-time site work only if needed and safe with gap-covering pay.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about uncertain later income, even with a decade to prepare.
S4.quote: A carpentry apprentice can learn more from one corrected drawing than from a perfect sample.
fieldNote: She does not treat **age sixty-eight** as an automatic paid retirement date.
Post-2036 **site work** remains conditional on the actual budget gap, a posted local role and safe, adequate pay.

steps.text: Keep leading repair jobs and recording awkward measurements for apprentices
Add from full pay packets to savings only after bills are covered
Apply after 2036 for posted safe local part-time work only if needed at gap-covering pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because site plans could change quickly and capable robots around 2031 might cut the last wages we counted on. A paid safe trial, funded recognised training with paid release and a posted local inspector job at bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who decides that a robot's trial has failed. The person on the building site needs authority to stop unsafe work before a neat report is sent upstairs.

portrait: **Grace**, fifty-eight, leads repair carpentry and general building work with a vocational trade certificate.
She has **typical trade pay**, a partner, grown children, a few months saved and some alternative nearby builders.
She uses **AI daily** for material lists but checks site measurements and wants paid, supervised trials before trusting new equipment.
The **2028** case threatens planned wages most; longer cases allow funded quality training and a check of her retirement budget.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change plans immediately and bring capable building robots around 2031, threatening her remaining paid years.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid safe trial**, funded recognised training with paid release and a posted local inspector job at bill-covering wages would help.
headlineQuote: The person on the building site needs authority to stop unsafe work before a neat report is sent upstairs.
